records.title: Historic El Niño drives extreme eastern Pacific warmth and a forecast record share of the ocean in marine heatwave
records.description: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center says on 8 October 2026 that El Niño continues to strengthen, with eastern equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures more than 4.0C above average in places. NOAA's marine heatwave forecast gives eastern tropical Pacific heatwave likelihood above 90% through winter 2026-27, and global coverage is forecast to reach 45%.

location.name: Eastern tropical Pacific and global ocean
location.detail: Eastern equatorial Pacific El Niño region with global marine heatwave coverage effects

records.layer_rationale: Basin-scale ocean heating from a developing El Niño is a physical climate condition.

notes.harm: Heatwave exposure is forecast rather than a documented mortality event; subsurface anomalies above +10C persist in the eastern Pacific (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources documents closures or fishery losses from this event so far (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: NOAA puts 38% of the global ocean in heatwave in August 2026 and forecasts 45% for winter (ref 3).
notes.duration: Copernicus recorded heatwaves over about 82% of the ocean by end of June, and NOAA forecasts them through winter 2026-27 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: CPC has an El Niño Advisory in effect and gives 83% for a historic event in October-December (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: CPC: 83% chance of a historic El Niño (above +2.5C on the 3-month RONI) for October-December 2026; Nino-3.4 at +2.1C.

measures.name: Global ocean in marine heatwave, August 2026
Forecast global marine heatwave coverage, winter 2026-27

trend.note: CPC says El Niño continues to strengthen (ref 1).

records.public_contact: NOAA Climate Prediction Center, contact details on cpc.ncep.noaa.gov
corrective_actions: CPC issued an El Niño Advisory and continues monthly updates (ref 1).

records.title: Record king tide flooding in Broward and Miami-Dade, with higher tides forecast through November
records.description: Unusually high king tides flooded streets across Broward and Miami-Dade counties on 26-27 September 2026, and a coastal flood advisory was issued. Port Everglades recorded its highest flooding since the gauge was installed in 2018. Further king tide windows run through October and November.

location.name: Port Everglades to Miami Beach, Florida
location.detail: Broward and Miami-Dade counties, southeast Florida

records.layer_rationale: Tidal flooding of a low-lying coast made more frequent by sea level rise.

notes.harm: Saltwater covered the Hollywood Broadwalk and nearly reached street level on Collins Avenue, but NWS had no reports of water entering homes or businesses (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Fort Lauderdale police closed about two miles of A1A because of flooding (ref 1).
notes.scale: The event affected two counties on one stretch of coast, below regional-sea scale (ref 1).
notes.duration: King tide windows recur through 24-30 October and into November, and the city lists six fall windows in 2026 (ref 2).
notes.significance: A coastal flood advisory was issued, a formal notice (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Tide about 2 feet above normal at Port Everglades and Virginia Key, highest at Port Everglades since the station began in 2018, topping Hurricane Nicole (2022).

measures.name: Tide height above normal high tide
measures.note: Port Everglades and Virginia Key, 27 September 2026 report (ref 1).

measures.name: Sea level rise over past 30 years
measures.note: Figure as stated in the news report (ref 1).

signals: Road closure of about two miles of A1A (ref 1).

trend.note: Report says the next king tide period is forecast to be the year's highest (ref 1).

corrective_actions: Hollywood is testing removable storm panels at seawall openings on South Lake Drive (ref 1).
Miami takes flooding reports online and by 311 (ref 2).

sources.title: South Florida King Tides Flood Streets, Break Records
sources.basis: News citing the Miami Herald and National Weather Service

records.title: Arctic sea ice minimum ties tenth lowest and Antarctic winter peak is third lowest in 2026
records.description: NASA reports the Arctic minimum on 12 September 2026 was about 4.6 million square km, tied for tenth lowest, and the 20 lowest minimums all fall in 2007-2026. Provisional NSIDC data put the Antarctic winter peak at 17.59 million square km on 14 September, third lowest in the satellite record.

location.name: Arctic Ocean and Southern Ocean sea ice

records.layer_rationale: Loss of polar sea ice is a physical climate change.

notes.harm: The Barents Sea recorded its earliest melt-out on record, an ecosystem-relevant ice loss without a documented mortality (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The opened reports describe no closures or economic restrictions (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Both polar oceans are covered, with the Antarctic winter peak third lowest in 48 years (ref 2).
notes.duration: NASA says all 20 lowest Arctic minimums occurred from 2007 to 2026 (ref 1).
notes.significance: Agency reporting only; no listing, order or advisory is involved (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Arctic minimum about 4.6 million sq km on 12 September 2026, tied for tenth lowest; Antarctic peak 17.59 million sq km on 14 September (provisional), third lowest.

measures.name: Antarctic winter peak extent (provisional)
measures.note: NSIDC provisional data via Carbon Brief (ref 2).

trend.note: NSIDC scientist Walt Meier: the Arctic has plateaued but remains low relative to earlier years (ref 1).

responsible_bodies.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

sources.title: Concerning low sea ice persists as Antarctic hits third-lowest winter peak
sources.basis: News citing NSIDC data and scientists

records.title: At least 12 of 15 stranded pygmy killer whales dead on Ninety Mile Beach, New Zealand
records.description: Fifteen pygmy killer whales stranded on Ninety Mile Beach in New Zealand's Far North District on 1 October 2026, and at least 12 were found dead. The whales were spread over several kilometres of beach, and rough conditions hampered the rescue. Officials said they were still working to understand the full circumstances of the stranding.

location.name: Ninety Mile Beach, Far North District
location.detail: West coast of the Far North District, North Island, New Zealand

records.layer_rationale: A mass stranding and mortality of a marine mammal species.

notes.harm: At least 12 of the 15 stranded pygmy killer whales were found dead (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The reports describe no closure, advisory or economic disruption (ref 1).
notes.scale: The whales were spread over several kilometres of a single beach (ref 1).
notes.duration: The stranding was reported on a Thursday and burial of the dead was under way the next day (ref 1).
notes.significance: The reports cite a conservation agency response but no formal notice, listing or enforcement action (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: At least 12 of 15 stranded pygmy killer whales were found dead.

records.public_contact: Department of Conservation's published general channel
corrective_actions: Conservation officials and volunteers launched a rescue effort; burial of the dead whales was under way (ref 1).

sources.publisher: The Star (Anadolu Agency, citing Radio New Zealand)

records.title: NOAA public comment on a 65,000 km2 deep-seabed nodule mining application in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone
records.description: NOAA found a consolidated exploration licence and commercial recovery permit application from TMC USA in full compliance with US deep seabed mining law and opened a public comment period running to 19 October 2026, with a virtual hearing on 13 October. Certification and an environmental impact statement would follow if NOAA certifies the application.

location.name: Clarion-Clipperton Zone, central Pacific
location.type: Deep seabed mineral area beyond national jurisdiction
location.detail: Polymetallic nodule area between Hawaii and Mexico, outside any national jurisdiction.

records.layer_rationale: A national permitting process for mining the high seabed outside the international regime.

notes.harm: Potential seabed habitat disturbance only; no environmental impact statement has yet been prepared and NOAA says one follows certification (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or coastal-livelihood disruption is reported in the cited coverage (ref 1).
notes.scale: A single mining province in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a regional-scale area of the Pacific (ref 1).
notes.duration: The application was filed on 6 February 2026 and review has run for months (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal Federal Register notice with a 60-day comment period and a public hearing (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Public comment period 19 August to 19 October 2026; virtual public hearing 13 October 2026, 3-5 p.m. ET.

measures.name: Comment period length
measures.note: Federal Register comment period ending 19 October 2026 (ref 1).

signals: The applicant is a US-listed deep-sea mining developer; no market data in the cited sources (ref 1).

responsible_bodies.name: NOAA National Ocean Service, deep seabed mining programme

records.public_contact: NOAA deep seabed mining page lists the docket and hearing registration.
corrective_actions: NOAA opened public comment and a virtual hearing before deciding on certification.

records.title: Nairobi Convention COP12 opens in Dar es Salaam on its 40th anniversary to set Western Indian Ocean governance priorities
records.description: The twelfth Conference of the Parties to the Nairobi Convention met in Dar es Salaam on 6-9 October 2026 with its ten Contracting Parties. Tanzania set priorities including national law and enforcement, coastal ecosystem restoration and marine pollution; adopted decisions are not reported in the cited sources.

location.name: Western Indian Ocean region
location.detail: Meeting held in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania; Convention covers ten Contracting Parties.

records.layer_rationale: Regional treaty process for ocean governance.

notes.harm: No specific harm is documented in the cited meeting coverage (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited coverage says more than 65 million people depend directly on the ocean but reports no disruption (ref 1).
notes.scale: The Convention covers the Western Indian Ocean region with ten Contracting Parties (ref 2).
notes.duration: The Convention dates from 1985 and the meeting marks 40 years of governance work (ref 1).
notes.significance: A formal treaty COP reviewing the 2025-2035 Integrated Regional Programme and 2025-2028 Programme of Work (ref 2).

population_affected.note: People depending directly on the ocean in the region, per the cited article (ref 1).

key_measure.text: Ocean wealth valued at over $300 billion; more than 65 million people depend directly on the ocean.

signals: Tourism is about 70% of the region's estimated $20.8 billion annual economic output (ref 1).

records.public_contact: Nairobi Convention Secretariat via the UNEP COP12 page.
corrective_actions: Parties review the Integrated Regional Programme 2025-2035 and Programme of Work 2025-2028.

records.title: Crude oil leaking from grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi reaches Oman's coast
records.description: The tanker Caroline Bezengi, reported to carry around 800,000 barrels of Russian crude, has been disabled near the Al Hallaniyat Islands off Oman and has leaked oil since the summer. Omani authorities put the slick at nearly 400 square kilometres and confirmed oil on mainland beaches at Ras Madrakah in mid-August; Greenpeace estimated about 1,300 square kilometres. A salvage operation began on 13 August 2026; the sources opened for this record do not report the situation after mid-August.

location.name: Al Hallaniyat Islands to Ras Madrakah, Oman
location.detail: Arabian Sea coast of Oman, off the Hallaniyat archipelago marine reserve; oil reported on the Ras Madrakah shoreline and expected on southern Masirah Island

records.layer_rationale: Crude oil released into coastal waters from a grounded tanker.

notes.harm: Oil reached beaches at Ras Madrakah, affecting up to 40 km of coastline, near a marine reserve created last year for sea turtles; no casualty counts are reported (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources reports a fishery closure or lost catch; the vessel lies about 22 nautical miles off the fishing village of Sharbithat (ref 2).
notes.scale: Omani authorities put the slick at nearly 400 sq km around one archipelago and a stretch of mainland coast; Greenpeace's 1,300 sq km estimate is still within one national coast (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The tanker was disabled on 8 June and grounded on 30 June, and was still leaking at the 12 to 14 August reports, so the release has run for more than two months (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The IMO publicly confirmed monitoring and oil spill contingency planning, and Oman's Environment Authority is running response operations (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Omani authorities: spill measured nearly 400 square kilometres; Greenpeace: about 1,300 square kilometres as of 12 August 2026.

measures.name: Slick area (Greenpeace, satellite)
measures.note: Grew from 45 sq km in late July (ref 3).

signals: No fishery or tourism loss is reported in the opened sources.

trend.note: Reports opened run from 12 to 14 August 2026; none newer was found, so the current state is unconfirmed.

records.public_contact: Oman Environment Authority public enquiries (see published website)
corrective_actions: Ambrey announced a salvage operation with Omani authorities on 13 August 2026, with specialists aboard to stabilise the cargo (ref 3).
Oman's Environment Authority reports monitoring and response teams prioritising sensitive areas (ref 1).
